item.title: Germany's Merz attacks AfD in stormy debate after far-right election win
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c98679wr78do?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Germany's Merz attacks AfD in stormy debate after far-right election win - Published German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has clashed with AfD leader Alice Weidel in parliament, calling her party a "destructive force" with a migration policy that amounts to "ethnic cleansing" for skilled workers. Merz was addressing the Bundestag in the aftermath of the anti-immigration party's sweeping victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt where it won almost 44% of the vote, while the chancellor's conservatives saw their vote halved. Weidel told MPs that voters had shown that Merz's coalition with the centre left was a total failure and his time was up. Merz hit back saying the AfD had harmed German interests by backing Russia, and its "remigration" policy would affect millions. It is not yet clear whether the party will be able to form a government or not in Saxony-Anhalt, having fallen three seats short of an outright majority. No far-right party has won power in any of Germany's 16 states since World War Two, and Merz has admitted the "seismic" result has changed Germany. The AfD's success has been praised by US President Donald Trump, who said "the Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night", linking the victory to "absolutely horrible immigration rules and regulations". The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been labelled as "right-wing extremist" by German domestic intelligence and the party has promised a "deportation and remigration" offensive targeting irregular migrants. Trump had been due to speak by phone to the German chancellor on Wednesday to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in the US, but the government spokesman in Berlin said the call had been postponed without saying why. No new date has been set. Repeatedly heckled by AfD MPs, the chancellor told Weidel that one in six skilled workers had a migration background, and if her party had its way then its policy would amount to "nothing other than an ethnic cleansing in the skilled trades based on skin colour and origin". While the government understood some deportations were needed, he said it made a careful distinction between those who contributed to German prosperity and those without permanent residency. Disruption by AfD MPs became so loud that at one point Bundestag President Julia Klöckner threatened to start expelling people from the chamber: "We are not on a football pitch." Weidel said mass migration had left Germans with daily knife violence and attacks on trains and in stations, but Merz warned that the AfD's plans would mean that no single care home, hospital or restaurant could function. As leader of the main opposition party in the Bundestag, Weidel opened the session by telling Merz his Christian Democrats had been "pulverised" in Saxony-Anhalt, after winning 17.2% of the vote, and she accused his government with the Social Democrats of driving Germany towards bankruptcy. Merz said her party had not won an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt and it would not achieve one in Germany. "You are and will remain a destructive force," he said, accusing the party of cheating the voters by saying before the election that their candidate for premier, Ulrich Siegmund, would only rule if he won a majority, but hours after the vote deciding to go and find one. The AfD has opened the door to working with another party, perhaps the left-wing populist BSW, as long as it backs Siegmund to be state premier. Siegmund's number two in Saxony-Anhalt, has even suggested that Merz's CDU could work with his party, if it abandons the so-called firewall (Brandmauer), under which no mainstream party will work with the far right. - Published2 days ago

item.title: Oil hits $100 a barrel for first time since July after US and Houthi strikes
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cyvznqypz0yo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Oil hits $100 a barrel for first time since July after US and Houthi strikes - Published Oil prices rose past $100 (£74) a barrel on Wednesday after further strikes in the conflict between the US and Iran and continuing Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia. In back and forth attacks, the US hit five Iranian tankers in reprisal strikes after Tehran targeted one of its warships. Brent crude - which is the global benchmark for prices - has not been as expensive since the end of July, when a ceasefire between Iran and the US collapsed. Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement also attacked oil facilities in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday and have been targeting tankers in the Red Sea. Brent crude did dip back down to $99.90 a barrel, but any fresh flare-ups in the Middle East could see it pushed higher again. Tit-for-tat strikes between Iran and the US have escalated in the past week, more than six months after conflict broke out when the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran on 28 February. Oil prices have fluctuated wildly since the war began, and pressure on the industry has been exacerbated by wider regional instability. Before the conflict Brent crude had been priced at about $70 (£52) a barrel. But the war has seen the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which carries 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG). The rising costs have sparked huge price leaps in petrol around the world for motorists at the pumps. The US strikes on the five Iranian tankers saw four in the Gulf of Oman linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) hit as well as another near Kharg Island. Tehran responded by launching missiles at a US base in Jordan - most of which were shot down - and said it attacked two US vessels and eight oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. The Houthis and Saudi Arabia have also been exchanging strikes since July after their own informal ceasefire unravelled. On Monday the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing a prison in al-Hazm and killing 11 people. Then on Tuesday the Saudi authorities said Houthis had struck civilian and economic sites in the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran. The latest round of escalation comes after Iran targeted a US warship with ballistic missiles, which Centcom said were "successfully evaded". It added that no American troops were harmed during the attacks. In response, the US said that the five Iranian oil tankers it targeted were "part of a multi-billion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies". One of the ships it had struck, the M/T Riesco, sunk in the Gulf of Oman, Centcom later said, posting a video on X of the damaged vessel. Kharg Island - where one Iranian tanker was attacked in the latest round of US strikes - hosts Iran's main terminal for exporting oil. Some 90% of the country's crude oil passes through the island in the Gulf, transported through pipes from the mainland. Also on Tuesday, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement attacked energy facilities and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, injuring 73 people, according to Saudi authorities. The drone and missile attack caused fires at oil facilities and installations that led to a temporary halt in operations, Saudi Arabia's military and energy ministry said. When asked by reporters about the latest tit-for-tat strikes between the US and Iran, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday said the situation was "pretty straightforward". "Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships. And, for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers. And I think you'll see that again today," Rubio told reporters during a trip in Colombia. The US strikes on Tuesday came hours after Iran's Navy claimed it had seized an uncrewed US submarine in the Strait of Hormuz. US Navy Capt Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Centcom, said that the "underwater drone operated by US forces malfunctioned more than a day ago" and was used to survey regional waters "in support of ongoing operations". The defective drone was "an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment", he said, adding that US operations in regional waters were ongoing. With additional reporting from Peter Hoskins. Related topics - Published3 days ago - Published2 days ago

item.title: US to ban imports of some Canadian alcohol, dairy goods and motorbikes
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c99dm1000p7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US to ban imports of some Canadian alcohol, dairy goods and motorbikes - Published The US will ban imports of a range of Canadian products, including alcoholic spirits, some dairy goods and motorbikes, after its neighbour's retaliatory tariffs on American goods came into force. In a series of executive orders on Tuesday, President Donald Trump said Canada was "discriminating" against the US and outlined the bans, which will begin on 29 September. Officials on both sides have said they would like to strike a trade deal, but no new talks have been scheduled since negotiations collapsed in late August. Dominic LeBlanc, Canada's trade minister, said the latest US measures were "unjustified" and that he would work to protect the country's workers, families and businesses. "Our core focus is on what we can control: building strength at home, diversifying our partnerships abroad, and building Canada strong for all Canadians," LeBlanc said. He said he had contacted his US counterpart and promised to work "in good faith" to resolve tensions. Earlier on Tuesday, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a video address that his country's move away from the US as its largest trading partner "will come at a cost". The White House's new sanctions are the latest strike in a months-long trade war between the US and Canada. The two countries have historically been close allies, with each a key business partner to the other. Generally more than two-thirds of Canada's total exports go to the US. In 2025, Canada's exports of alcoholic spirits to the US were worth US$687m (£507m), dairy products were worth $269m and motorbikes were worth $90m, according to UN data compiled by Trading Economics. But Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics, said the import ban covered just 0.25% of Canada's exports to the US. He said: "Nonetheless, Trump's willingness to impose an import ban is further evidence, if it were needed, that these latest measures are about inflicting economic pain rather than raising revenue." - What tariffs will really cost Canadians and Americans - Published2 hours ago - The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts - Published31 August Canada is the second-largest trading partner of the US after Mexico. Its exports are less diversified than those of the US. In recent months, business owners on both sides of the border have expressed fears over the trade war's fallout. Many expect prices of goods to rise and the number of customers to fall. Last month, the White House imposed 50% tariffs on around $20bn (£14.8bn) of Canadian goods after several rounds of talks had broken down. Those tariffs hit sectors including Canada's furniture and wine industries, as well as some sporting and fishing equipment businesses. Canada responded with what Carney called "dollar-for-dollar" tariffs on US goods like steel, clothing and furniture. The counter-duties came into effect after midnight on Tuesday. Canada is "discriminating" against US businesses by restricting American goods while not doing the same to the same products from other countries, the White House said when announcing the new import restrictions on Tuesday. Some products, like whey and non-alcoholic beer, have been banned from import entirely, while tariffs have been further hiked for others, including for cheeses and cheese substitutes - which were not covered by bans - and for motorboats. The list of Canadian products banned by the White House include: - Some dairy products like whey - Cane molasses - Non-alcoholic beer - A long list of wine, rum and vodka products - Beer made from malt - Motorbikes, including mopeds Those facing higher import taxes include: - Various types of cheese - Raw hides and skins - Paper - Some furniture and mattresses - Some metals, including aluminium and iron - Motorboats - Golf carts - Fishing rod parts and accessories - Switchboards Washington has targeted "significant industries" for Canada, including its politically influential dairy businesses, said economics lecturer Scott French from the University of New South Wales in Australia. Trump has previously argued that Canada's system - which has production quotas, set pricing, and import limits on dairy, eggs, and poultry - is unreasonable to US farmers. - Canada's 'powerful' dairy sector is in Trump's trade crosshairs - Published23 July The import bans and new tariffs will also put Canada's leaders under more pressure to resist Trump's demands for concessions, French said. The trade war will be "costly for both sides due to the historical level of integration of the North American economy," he said, adding that consumers on both sides will end up as "the biggest losers". On Monday, Trump hinted at more trade restrictions to come, warning Canadian aircraft company Bombardier that it would no longer be able to sell its products in the US unless it moved manufacturing there. Trump has long believed that tariffs will help reduce trade imbalances between the US and other countries, but his wide-ranging levies have upset many of the States' traditional allies. Some Canadians have led a massive boycott of US products like alcohol, which have vanished from some store shelves after Trump launched his global tariff campaign last year. Trade expert Deborah Elms, from the Hinrich Foundation, told the BBC the import ban could have a "strong" impact on any Canadian business with US buyers, though early estimates show a "modest impact" affecting around $1bn worth of goods. Canada will likely "hold course for now" and adjust their business support measures to account for the US' latest moves, Elms said. "The bigger question is what it will take for the two sides to sit back down together. The language in these proclamations, as an example, isn't helpful in getting to the negotiating table," she added. Carney said on Tuesday as Canada's counter-tariffs came into effect: "There's always a cost to action. But it doesn't come close to the cost of standing still." Tension between the US and Canada has also moved beyond tariffs. In August, Trump ordered Lake Ontario to be renamed as Lake America, resulting in uproar from Canadians and some in the US. item.title: Russia and Ukraine exchange strikes as two killed at Moldova border
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgyvpxe3yjo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Russia and Ukraine exchange strikes as two killed at Moldova border - Published Two people have been killed after Russian drones struck a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said. The Starokozache crossing, around 500km (310 miles) south of Kyiv, was closed after the overnight attack. Images from the scene showed several cars left completely scorched, with wreckage and debris strewn across the border post. Meanwhile, four people, including a child, were killed in the southern Russian city of Novorossiysk in a Ukrainian drone attack, the regional governor said. Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up long-range strikes in recent months, despite renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war. Zelensky renewed calls for international support in the wake of the Starokozache crossing attack, saying "the aggression must be stopped here and now before it spreads any further". The border link between Ukraine and Moldova was shut after the attack killed two people and injured three others, Odesa regional governor Oleg Kiper said. A Moldovan driver was also injured, according to the country's foreign ministry. Moldova has increasingly found itself caught up in the conflict, with Prime Minister Vasile Tofan confirming that 17 drones had struck Moldovan territory in August alone - more than during the whole of last year. "Those who ignore or downplay these threats - and refuse to name the aggressor - are denying reality," he wrote on social media. "Russia started this war. Russia alone bears responsibility." Russia's defence ministry said its forces had shot down 596 Ukrainian drones overnight. Novorossiysk – in the south of the country on the Black Sea coast - was hit hardest in what governor Veniamin Kondratiev described as a "massive overnight enemy drone attack". As well as the four deaths, 29 people were injured, and damage was reported to residential buildings, a church and a preschool. The strikes came a day after Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke to US President Donald Trump by phone about efforts to end the conflict. The Trump administration has been pressing for direct talks between Russia and Ukraine, with Kyiv saying they could take place this month. The Kremlin, however, has said it is too early to discuss a date or venue. The call followed talks between US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff and Putin in Moscow, before the pair travelled to Kyiv for meetings with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. item.title: N Korea has built two-storey uranium enrichment facility, says watchdog
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy0zqk2w92lo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
N Korea has built two-storey uranium enrichment facility, says watchdog - Published North Korea has built a new two-storey uranium enrichment facility, the head of the world's nuclear watchdog said this week, calling it a cause for "serious concern". The new building is part of the main Yongbyon nuclear complex, and reportedly capable of housing up to 28 centrifuge cascades used to enrich uranium. In a report published late last month, the International Atomic Energy Agency said Pyongyang has also begun operating an expanded annex at another enrichment site. These findings point to a steady expansion of the North's sancitoned nuclear infrastructure. The agency, which has no inspectors in North Korea since it was expelled in 2009, relies on satellite imagery for assessments. "The continuation and further development of the DPRK's nuclear programme are clear violations of relevant UN Security Council resolutions and are deeply regrettable," IAEA director Rafael Grossi said in a statement earlier this week. The IAEA first referred to the existence of the building in June, although Grossi had mentioned the possibility earlier in the year. In June, the agency said that North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited a "newly inaugurated nuclear materials production factory" on 3 June, which it identified as the Yongbyon enrichment facility. Kim had praised the country's "greatly expanded production capacity", adding that this would "offer the possibility of carrying out larger plans", according to the agency's report. Despite running one the poorest countries in the world, Kim spends millions each year developing a secretive nuclear arsenal. A 2022 report by a non-proliferation think-tank put this figure at $640m. "What makes North Korea's nuclear programme so concerning is that many of its facilities are unknown, concealed, and thus difficult to target," Edward Howell, a lecturer at the University of Oxford told the BBC. "Beyond Yongbyon, we know that other facilities exist: Kangson, for instance. The embeddedness of North Korea's nuclear doctrine within its foreign and domestic policy means that we should expect there to be more concealed production sites." The agency also said there were indications that operations had started at another enrichment facility in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, in January this year. An annex had first been constructed in Kangson in 2024, it said. It had said in April that North Korea appeared to be stepping up its ability to make nuclear bombs, saying they were monitoring the apparent expansion of Yongbyon. The North's nuclear programme has accelerated under Kim, who has overseen a record number of missile tests. The country has fired has numerous intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) since it began testing its long-range system in 2017. The country has conducted six nuclear weapons tests so far, the last of which was in September 2017. In August, South Korea's president, Lee Jae Myung, proposed talks with North Korea on officially ending the war between the two countries, adding that this could serve as a forum for discussing "effective ways to halt the advancement of the North's nuclear capabilities". North Korea has yet to respond to the proposal. North Korea declared itself a nuclear power in 2022 and vowed never to relinquish its weapons, of which it is estimated to possess dozens. Lee previously said Pyongyang was producing 15 to 20 more warheads annually, telling the BBC last year he would back a deal between US President Donald Trump and Kim to freeze production. Additional reporting by Koh Ewe - Published8 March 2022 - Published28 February 2019

item.title: Uganda pulling out of Prince Harry's Invictus Games, says military chief
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3d7pzyjzllo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Uganda pulling out of Prince Harry's Invictus Games, says military chief - Published Uganda is pulling out of the Invictus Games, a sports event for wounded military veterans run by the Duke of Sussex, only two months after the country said it would join. General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, chief of defence and son of the president, made the announcement in a social media post on X. He said the decision to withdraw from the games was "in order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III". Ugandan government spokesman Alan Kasujja confirmed this to the BBC: "General Kainerugaba decides whether or not the UPDF [Uganda People's Defence Force] participates in the Invictus Games. What you saw is his stated position. If it changes, he will let the world know." - King makes clear Harry and Meghan remain non-working royals - Published1 day ago - Prince Harry and Meghan land in UK days after announcing move - Published26 August The Ugandan military chief's announcement follows a letter sent this week on behalf of the King which made clear that Prince Harry and Meghan, who have now returned to the UK, were not working royals. A report in The Times newspaper quoted the general's concerns about the "Harry-Meghan nonsense", suggesting this was the background to the decision. "In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games," said the general in an overnight post. "We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty's approval." However, royal sources have said that the King encourages all projects which support wounded service personnel. A spokesman for the Invictus Games said they had not received any official information about a potential withdrawal and have been seeking clarification from their contacts in Uganda. Among other posts on X from General Kainerugaba on Thursday was one that read: "I consider myself the most handsome, most daring and glorious Commander who ever lived." There was also a series of angry messages about other generals who had danced without his permission. The participation of Uganda in the next games, to be held next year in Birmingham, was announced in July, when Prince Harry was in London promoting the sports event, which celebrates the resilience and rehabilitation of wounded military men and women. Uganda had become the 26th country to take part in the games. Sign up here to get the latest royal stories and analysis every week with our Royal Watch newsletter. item.title: Colombia's new president loosens gun control rules
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqlwekrl3dqo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Colombia's new president loosens gun control rules - Published Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has signed a decree which eases restrictions on people carrying legal firearms in public. De la Espriella, who during his campaign for the presidency promised to take an iron-fist approach to crime, said it was "not right that criminals are armed to the teeth while decent people can't defend themselves". The decree lifts a suspension that had been in force for a decade, which meant that even those in possession of a permit to carry guns could not do so without additional authorisation. De la Espriella insisted that the decree would not create a free-for-all and that tight controls over who can own a gun would remain in place. While signing the decree, the president said he had made good on his campaign promise: "A man's word is his honour, and I have honour, that's why I keep my word." The restriction on carrying legal guns in public was brought in by the then-President Juan Manuel Santos in December 2015. It was originally meant to be a temporary measure, aimed at improving security during the Christmas and New Year festivities. But the suspension was extended yearly by Santos and two subsequent presidents from opposing sides of the political spectrum: conservative Iván Duque and left-wing Gustavo Petro. Under the law, even those with a permit to carry a gun could not take it out of their homes unless they applied for - and were granted - additional authorisation. De la Espriella has insisted that his decree has removed a restriction which had never been meant to be permanent. According to Spanish newspaper El País, the decree will affect almost 700,000 people in Colombia who are already in possession of a legal permit to carry a gun. They will now be able to take their registered gun out of their home, provided their permits remain up to date. Green Alliance Party Senator Ariel Ávila described the move as a "grave error", arguing that legally held guns would end up in the hands of criminals. Ávila insisted that it created an ethical dilemma, as it should only be state forces that carry guns and act as guarantors of people's security. De la Espriella insisted that the measure would not negatively affect security in the country and said forces were targeting those holding illegal guns and had seized more than 15,000 firearms so far this year. Most of them, according to de la Espriella, belonged to members of breakaway factions of the Farc rebel group and the Gulf Clan criminal gang. Related topics - Published27 August

item.title: Family of killed teen call for death penalty in D4vd trial
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62mn90ppnro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Family of killed teen call for death penalty in D4vd trial - Published The family of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez has lobbied for the death penalty if D4vd is found guilty murdering their daughter. D4vd, who was born David Anthony Burke, is charged with killing the teenager, whose dismembered body was found in the trunk of a Tesla car registered to his address on 8 September 2025. Burke has pleaded not guilty to the charges. The death penalty is under a temporary ban in California, where Burke is due to stand trial, but in a statement Hernandez' family said execution "would be perfect" if the singer was convicted of murder. In a related development, Hernandez's parents filed a civil lawsuit against Burke on Friday, seeking monetary damages including burial and funeral expenses. The lawsuit, lodged at Los Angeles Superior Court and reported by multiple, external US media outlets, external, makes similar claims to those raised by prosecutors in the criminal case against the singer. Mercedes Martinez and Jesus Rivas allege that Burke caused the wrongful death, false imprisonment and childhood sexual assault of their daughter. In the court documents, they say Burke and Hernandez first met in November 2023, when she was 13 years old. Over the next 16 months, they claim, the pair would exchange almost 10,000 texts and have sex several times. "At all relevant times Burke was an adult who occupied a position of authority over decedent, a minor, and was able to and did exercise undue influence and control over her," the parents say, in papers filed last Friday. They go on to claim that Burke killed the teenager at his Hollywood Hills home, when she threatened to reveal their relationship, after allegedly sending a message that read: "I will end ur career and ur life". In addition to Burke, the lawsuit names several of Burke's companies and managers, his mother and a live-in security guard. Hernandez's parents allege that these people "enabled Burke to isolate" Rivas Hernandez and facilitated his travel, housing and security. Burke's management company Mogul Vision and finance manager have previously denied knowing about Burke and Rivas Hernandez, the Los Angeles Times, external reported. In July, a judge found enough probable cause for Burke to stand trial on the murder charge in the criminal case. At the time, the district attorney said he was weighing whether to seek the death penalty. In a statement on Monday, which would have been Hernandez's 16th birthday, her family demanded that Burke be subjected to execution. "If the death penalty were activated, it would be perfect for this kind of human being, devoid of feelings and emptiness inside, and without conscience, who only caused pain to our daughter, our family, and the world that supports our precious daughter," read the statement, released via the family's attorney. Burke again pleaded not guilty to the charges last week and has since parted ways with his celebrity defence attorney. He is now being represented by a public defender and is due back in court on 19 October. His trial has been moved to next year. Deputy public defender Walid Kandeel has said that Burke was "entitled to a defence that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence". "We are committed to providing him with that defence," he said. His office did not immediately provide comment on the civil lawsuit. - Published31 August - Published28 July

item.title: White House pulls Tetris-style 'Build The Wall' game after copyright concern
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9v9djj4m3do?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
White House pulls Tetris-style 'Build The Wall' game after copyright concern - Published The White House has taken down a Tetris-style game on its website called "Build The Wall", days after The Tetris Company raised concerns over its use of the game's likeness. The game, which saw players stack blocks to build a wall to "protect the border" is one of five arcade games which have appeared on the White House website. On 4 September the official Tetris account on X posted, external the firm was "not involved in the creation" of the game and it took "copyright infringement very seriously". The White House has not responded to requests for comment from the BBC or given an official reason for the takedown. "At Tetris we believe in the power of connection and building people together, not dividing them," the firm said in its initial response to the game. "To our fans everywhere: we love you, we see you, and we're grateful to have you in our community." The Tetris Company has had previous success in suing firms for infringing on its copyright - settling for an undisclosed fee with the makers of the iPhone game Mino in 2012, which it claimed stole the look and feel of the block-builder. Four other arcade games still remain on the mini-game section of the White House website. "Flappy Bill", a clone of the 2013 viral hit Flappy Bird sees players fly a bald eagle and dodging monuments from the National Mall. Meanwhile in Rio Run, players must "patrol the line along the river", with gameplay reminiscent of the classic phone game Snake. When players run into the edge of the map, a "Deported" number shows how many people the player was able to catch. The games have drawn criticism from politicians, with Connecticut Democratic state senator Matt Lesser tweeting, external: "Heating oil is near an all-time high but hey you can play Border Tsar Tom Homan in a video game". Video games and The White House The arcade section is just one example of how the Trump administration has increasingly incorporated video game culture into its political messaging on social media. In October 2025, the official White House X account drew criticism for posting an AI-generated picture of President Trump, external in a suit from the video game Halo. Meanwhile on 6 March it posted a video which mixed footage of US military strikes in Iran with film and TV clips, as well a clip from Halo's protagonist Master Chief saying "finishing this fight". The post was condemned by the Master Chief voice actor Steve Downes in a now-deleted tweet which called for "the producers of this disgusting and juvenile war porn" to remove his voice from the video. The Pokémon Company International also criticised the White House's use of its imagery in March, when it included a tiny version of the popular character Pikachu in a meme posted online with the phrase "Make America Great Again". item.title: Baby orangutans found in Indian forest spark trafficking inquiry
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgynv90599o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Baby orangutans found in Indian forest spark trafficking inquiry - Published Five baby orangutans have been found in a forest in India's eastern state of Odisha, far from their natural habitat, prompting an investigation into how they got there. Photographs and videos widely shared online show the young apes sitting together on the forest floor and eating bananas, thousands of kilometres from the tropical rainforests where they belong. Orangutans are not native to India. The critically endangered apes are found in the wild only in Indonesia and Malaysia. Odisha's forest minister has said investigators are examining whether the animals were trafficked into the country by an international smuggling network and abandoned near a highway. The orangutans were rescued early on Tuesday in Balasore district after local people spotted them and alerted forest officials. They were given first aid before being taken to Nandankanan Zoological Park in the state capital, Bhubaneswar, where they are in quarantine and being monitored. Balasore District Forest Officer Pratik Prakash Indalkar told the BBC that the animals could not have reached Odisha naturally and may have been transported there by road. "The five animals were found in Ranakata, a proposed reserve forest in Bhogarai block, near the West Bengal border," he said. "The area is covered mainly by casuarina trees and is not a dense forest. It is also close to a state highway." The Odisha government has also reportedly asked India's Wildlife Crime Control Bureau to investigate. Police, forest officials and a special task force are involved in the inquiry. Forest officials believe the orangutans had been in the area for only two or three days. A search of the forest found no other orangutans or clues as to how the animals got there, Indalkar said. Officials described them to the BBC as infants, although some local reports suggest they are between one and two years old. Their young age makes their discovery particularly concerning, wildlife expert Biswajit Mohanty said. Young orangutans typically remain with their mothers for several years, learning the skills they need to survive independently. Females also reproduce slowly, usually giving birth only once every eight years. The discovery of five young orangutans together, thousands of kilometres from their natural habitat and with no adult animals nearby, has therefore raised concerns of how they came to be in Odisha. There are three known living species of orangutan - Bornean, Sumatran and Tapanuli - all of which are classified as critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, or IUCN. Over the years, their numbers have declined sharply because of deforestation, habitat loss and hunting. International commercial trade in orangutans is prohibited under Cites - the global agreement governing trade in endangered wildlife. They are also protected under Indian wildlife laws. Despite this, orangutans continue to be trafficked for sale as exotic pets and to private collectors. This is not the first time young orangutans have been found in India. In 2022, two baby orangutans were found abandoned at a checkpoint near the border between the states of Assam and Mizoram. Officials suspected they had been brought into India through neighbouring Myanmar.

item.title: Tycoon to pay ex-wife $1.87bn in record South Korea divorce settlement
item.description:

========================================
Tycoon to pay ex-wife $1.87bn in record South Korea divorce settlement - Published A South Korean court has ordered gaming tycoon Kwon Hyuk-bin to pay his ex-wife 2.55tr won ($1.87bn; £1.38bn) in assets, marking the largest divorce settlement in the country's history. Kwon, who founded South Korea's third-largest video game company Smilegate, is one of the country's richest men. Bloomberg puts his net worth at $3bn. Smilegate was wholly owned by him until Wednesday when a court ruled that a 35% stake, valued at about 2.5tr won, be transferred to his wife Lee Hwa-jin. He was also ordered to pay her an additional 65bn won in cash. This settlement is more than double the previous record of 944bn won which tech titan Chey Tae-won was ordered to pay his ex-wife. In filing for divorce with Kwon, Lee had sought a 50% stake in Smilegate. Her lawyers argued that she had helped finance the company at its founding, according to Bloomberg. Kwon and Lee got married in 2001, a year before he founded Smilegate. Its best-known titles include the first-person shooter game CrossFire and the action role-playing game Lost Ark. Lee also said she spent more than 20 years raising their children and caring for their household. Kwon in turn argued that Lee neither invested nor worked for the company. Earlier this year, Smilegate published a statement saying all of the company's initial capital came from Kwon. A Smilegate spokesperson declined to "comment on the major shareholder's personal matters". "We will continue to faithfully perform our duties as usual," they said in a statement cited by The Chosun Daily. Both parties can still challenge the ruling. In July this year, Chey Tae-won, the chairman of the corporate giant SK Group, was ordered to pay his ex-wife 944bn won which, prior to today's ruling, was the largest divorce award in Korean history. However, this was later struck down by the Supreme Court who cited a miscalculation that increased the value of the couple's assets. It has ordered the case to be reviewed.

item.title: 'You're not alone in the darkness': Gambia president urges calm after violent blackout protests
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgmr22kpd9yo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'You're not alone in the darkness': Gambia president urges calm after violent blackout protests - Published The Gambia's President Adama Barrow has urged citizens to remain calm over prolonged power cuts, saying the country is not alone in facing an electricity crisis that has affected several parts of West Africa. His comments follow protests on Monday night in the capital Banjul and surrounding areas over blackouts that residents say have sometimes lasted up to 48 hours. "When you lie down in the heat and the dark, believe that you are not alone in that darkness," Barrow said, pledging to boost power supplies by next month. The Gambia supplements its own generation with imported electricity, including supplies from Guinea and neighbouring Senegal. The tiny West African country has endured persistent blackouts since June, with outages becoming longer and more frequent during the current hot season as soaring temperatures drive up electricity demand. Frustration boiled over on Monday night, when protesters took to the streets in Banjul and surrounding areas, burning tyres and blocking roads over the prolonged power cuts. Police used tear gas to disperse crowds in Westfield area as they moved towards the headquarters of the national electricity company, Nawec, with some chanting. "Barrow must go". Protesters also gathered outside the vice-president's residence in Farato, where banners at an office of Barrow's ruling National People's Party were damaged. The unrest comes just months before a presidential election expected in December, in which Barrow is seeking a controversial third term. In a televised address on Tuesday night, Barrow acknowledged the hardship caused by the blackouts but warned protesters against damaging public infrastructure, saying it would only worsen the disruption and divert money towards repairs. "Let us not destroy in a moment of anger what we suffered so long to gain," he said. The president admitted there had been shortcomings in the government's planning, power generation and maintenance systems, calling the resulting outages "a national security issue" and an "emergency". "I know that the fans have stopped turning, children work in the dark, mothers throw away stale food, and the heat is unbearable by day and by night," the president, promising that supplies would improve by the end of October. He said a new 24-megawatt generating unit was being installed at the Brikama power station and would be commissioned by the end of next month. A contract has also been awarded for a 50MW solar power plant in Soma, although no completion date was given. "For a system of our size, this is considerable power, enough to make a big difference in your homes," Barrow added. The president visited facilities for the national energy utility on Tuesday morning and promised that The Gambia would receive new generators this week. Gallo Saidy, the Nawec chief, also appealed for patience, saying reduced electricity imports from the regional grid had contributed to the shortages. He said lower rainfall this year had reduced the electricity available through the regional network. "We are aware of the frustration and constraints that the Gambian people have," he said. "We are just asking The Gambian people to give us a little bit of time and patience." Nawec had warned in August that unusually high temperatures had driven a surge in electricity demand, while a technical problem had also affected a major generating unit supplying imported power.
